Difference (Differential) Amplifier using an Op-Amp

Subject: Analog Electronics  |  Unit: Operational Amplifier  |  Level: B.E./B.Tech ECE, GATE, core-company interviews

Objectives: derive Vout of a difference amplifier • design for a required gain • read a Multisim oscilloscope result and diagnose a wiring error • solve GATE-style problems.

IntroductionCircuitWorkingSimulationEquationsSolved problemsGATEInterviewApplicationsQuizRevision

1. Introduction

A difference (subtractor) amplifier uses one op-amp and four resistors to amplify the difference V2−V1 of two voltages while rejecting what is common to both. It is the basic front end for bridge sensors and balanced lines.

Principle: negative feedback forces V−≈V+ (virtual short). The inverting path gives gain −R1/R4 on V1; the non-inverting path gives a divided and amplified V2. When R1/R4=R3/R2 the common-mode term cancels.

Prerequisites: Ohm's law, voltage divider, ideal op-amp rules, superposition. Terms: differential gain Ad, common-mode gain Acm, CMRR=|Ad/Acm|, virtual short, saturation.

Types: basic difference amp (this page), difference amp with input buffers, 3-op-amp instrumentation amplifier.

3. Working principle

  1. DC view: with V1=1.2 V, V2=0.4 V, all R=10 kΩ: V+=0.2 V → V−=0.2 V → I(R4)=0.1 mA → drop across R1=1 V → Vout=0.2−1.0=−0.8 V.
  2. AC view: the same algebra applies sample by sample; sources of equal amplitude and phase give Vout=0 (common-mode rejection).
  3. Assumptions: ideal op-amp (infinite gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance), matched resistors, output within the rails.

Advantages: one op-amp, simple, adjustable gain. Limitations: low and unequal input resistance, CMRR depends on resistor matching, changing gain needs two resistors changed together.

Misconceptions: (1) R3 can be tied anywhere on the V2 line – no, it must be at the + input node. (2) “Virtual ground” – only true for the inverting amplifier; here V−=V+≠0. (3) Equal AC sources always show a waveform at the output – they show zero.

4. Multisim simulation (your screenshot)

Channel A−106.430 mV

At 1 kHz, 234.043 ms is 0.043 of a cycle, so sin ≈ 0.2678. Then 0.4×0.2678 = 107.1 mV (V2) and 1.2×0.2678 = 321.4 mV (V1); the C/B ratio is exactly 3. So B = V2, C = V1 and A = Vout (also consistent with the wire colours: green, magenta, red; this mapping is an inference).

Discrepancy supported by the image: the schematic shows R3 joined at the V2 side of R2 (node 3), not at the + input (node 2). Then V+=V2 and Vout=2V2−V1. Prediction at the cursor: 2(107.122)−321.365 = −107.121 mV; measured −106.430 mV (difference ≈0.7 mV, a finite-gain/model effect). The intended V2−V1 would give −214.2 mV, which does not match. As built, Vout=−0.4 sin(ωt) V instead of −0.8 sin(ωt) V.
Fix: move the top end of R3 to the wire between R2 and the + pin.

The traces look small because Channel C is at 5 V/div (the A and B scales are not visible in the image, but their small amplitudes suggest similar settings). Use ≈0.5 V/div to see them clearly. Supply polarity and the op-amp model's saturation limits cannot be verified from this image.

5. Equations and derivation

V1→inverting via R4; R1 feedback; V2→R2→(+) with R3 to ground. Use superposition:

V+ = V2·R3/(R2+R3)  (V2 only)
Vout1 = −(R1/R4)·V1  (V1 only, + input grounded)
Vout2 = (1+R1/R4)·V+  (V2 only, non-inverting gain)
Vout = V2·[R3/(R2+R3)]·(1+R1/R4) − V1·R1/R4

If R1/R4=R3/R2=K then R3/(R2+R3)=K/(1+K) and:

Vout = K(V2−V1),  Ad=K,  Acm=0 (ideal),  CMRR(dB)=20·log10|Ad/Acm|

Limiting cases: K=1 → V2−V1; R3→∞ (open) → Vout=(1+K)V2−KV1; R3 on the V2 side (your screenshot) → V+=V2. Output limit: |Vout|≤Vsat (a bit below the rails). Resistor tolerance δ gives worst-case CMRR ≈ (1+Ad)/(4δ). Units: V in volts, R in ohms, gain dimensionless.

6. Solved problems

P1 (Easy) – all R = 10 kΩ, V1=1.2 V, V2=0.4 V. Find Vout.

Formula Vout=K(V2−V1), K=R1/R4=1. Vout=1×(0.4 V−1.2 V)=−0.8 V. Inside ±12 V, so no saturation.

P2 (Moderate) – R4=R2=10 kΩ, R1=R3=47 kΩ, V1=2.0 V, V2=2.3 V.

Balanced (47/10=47/10), K=4.7. Vout=4.7×(2.3−2.0)=4.7×0.3 V=1.41 V. The 2.15 V common-mode part is rejected. Shortcut: for balanced circuits, ignore the common level.

P3 (GATE-style, Difficult) – the screenshot circuit: R3 connected on the V2 side, all R=10 kΩ, V1=1.2 sinωt, V2=0.4 sinωt. Find Vout.

V+=V2 (R3 only loads the source). Vout=(1+1)V2−1·V1=0.8 sinωt−1.2 sinωt=−0.4 sinωt V (peak 0.4 V, inverted). Intended circuit: −0.8 sinωt V. Interpretation: a misplaced resistor halves the output and destroys common-mode rejection.

8. Core-company interview questions

1. What does a difference amplifier do and what is its output?It amplifies V2−V1 by R1/R4 when R1/R4=R3/R2. Follow-up: general formula with unmatched resistors (Section 5).
2. Why does resistor matching matter?Mismatch converts common-mode input into output. Worst-case CMRR ≈ (1+Ad)/(4δ); with 1 % resistors and Ad=1 that is ≈50 (≈34 dB). Use 0.1 % networks or laser-trimmed arrays.
3. What is the input resistance?Different at each input: the inverting side sees R4 (plus the effect of the other side); the + side sees R2+R3. Unequal and low, so source impedance imbalance degrades CMRR. Fix: buffer both inputs or use an instrumentation amp.
4. Debug: output is half of what you expect. What do you check?Check R3 placement (must be at the + node), then resistor values, feedback connection, supplies. In the simulation above, R3 on the V2 side gave 2V2−V1.
5. How do you measure CMRR in the lab?Tie both inputs together to one source: Acm=Vout/Vcm. Measure Ad with a differential input. CMRR=Ad/Acm, converted to dB.
6. Output stuck near a rail – why?Gain×difference exceeds the swing (e.g. gain 10, 1.5 V difference on ±12 V), or feedback is broken/open, or the supply is missing. A real LM741 saturates 1–2 V below the rails.
7. Why did DC operating-point analysis show a number while the scope shows a waveform?DC analysis uses DC values (or the AC source's DC offset, zero for a sine). Use Transient analysis for sinusoids and a DC source for a fixed −0.8 V result.
8. How does input offset voltage affect the output?It is amplified by the noise gain 1+R1/R4 (=2 here), so Vos of a few mV appears as a few mV of output error. Mitigate with a low-offset op-amp or offset trim.
9. What limits bandwidth?Closed-loop bandwidth ≈ GBW/(1+R1/R4). LM741 (GBW ≈1 MHz) gives roughly 500 kHz at gain-of-2 noise gain; slew rate limits large signals.
10. Why prefer an instrumentation amplifier for sensor bridges?High, balanced input impedance, high CMRR from an internally matched network, and a single gain-set resistor. Used in strain-gauge, ECG and pressure-sensor front ends.

Industry view: analog design, hardware validation and sensor-electronics teams use this stage for signal conditioning, and bench debugging of wiring and matching errors (as in Section 4) is a routine task.

9. Applications

  • Bridge-sensor conditioning (strain gauges, pressure sensors) before an ADC.
  • Balanced audio line receivers and ground-loop noise rejection.
  • Current sensing (high-side shunt measurement) and battery monitoring.
  • Subtractor in analog computation and PID error amplifiers.

Challenges: resistor tolerance, source-impedance imbalance, offset drift, saturation. Roles: analog/mixed-signal design, hardware test and validation, sensor/embedded interface engineer.
